title: Sitting an online assessment
objectives: Prepare for proctoring, retake rules, timing and the environment before an assessment starts.

screens.title: Before you click the link
screens.prose: An online assessment link arrives by email. You have a week. Sort what you would do before you click it. "Real link trial" means practising on the real link.

state.caption: Drag each card to Do or Do not.

screens.question: Sort the eight cards into Do and Do not.

hints.text: Which cards protect the one attempt you get?
The link in the email is the real test.
Do: tabs, charge, rules, webcam, check the paper rule. Do not: practise on the real link, café Wi-Fi, phone on the desk.

feedback.correct: Five things to do, three to avoid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which cards protect the one real attempt.

byKey.real: You put "Real link trial" in Do. The link is the test itself, and it usually works once.
byKey.cafe: Café Wi-Fi can drop mid-test. Use a connection you trust.
byKey.phone: A phone in view can look like help to a proctored test. Put it away.
byKey.tabs: Other tabs can trigger a proctoring flag and slow the machine. Close them.
byKey.charge: A laptop that dies mid-test ends the attempt. Charge it.
byKey.rules: The rules say what is allowed, such as a calculator. Read them first.
byKey.cam: A proctored test needs the webcam working throughout. Test it first.
byKey.paper: Some tests allow scrap paper and some do not. Ask or check the rules.

explain.text: Everything in Do protects one real attempt: the machine, the connection, the rules and the camera. The real link is never practice. Café Wi-Fi and a phone on the desk are the classic ways to lose it.

screens.prose: Your cards fall into four parts: **proctoring**, **retake rules**, **timing** and the **environment**. Check all four before any test.

rows: Webcam, screen and room may be watched or recorded
How many attempts, and how long before another
Items, minutes, and whether you can skip
Machine, connection, room, what is allowed on the desk

screens.question: "Test the webcam" belongs to which part?

options.why: Close: the webcam is part of your set-up. But you test it because the test watches you, which is proctoring.
Timing is items and minutes. The webcam is about being watched.
Retake rules are about attempts. The webcam is about being watched.

hints.text: Why does the test need your webcam?
Someone, or software, checks you are alone.
That is proctoring.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask why the camera matters.

explain.text: A proctored test watches you through the webcam and sometimes the screen. The other three parts are attempts, the clock and your set-up. One checklist covers all four.

screens.prose: Retake rules vary. One trading firm's official rule, in l4, is no reset or retake within 8 months (read October 2026). Say you sit its test on 15 November 2026 and fail.
screens.question: When could you sit it again?

options.why: You allowed one month. The rule is 8 months.
You counted 4 months. The rule is 8.
You used 12 months, a wait candidates often report at other firms. This rule is 8.

hints.text: Count 8 months on from November.
December is 1, January 2, and so on.
November plus 8 months is July: 15 July 2027.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count 8 months from 15 November.

explain.text: Eight months from 15 November 2026 is 15 July 2027, about when summer 2028 postings open. So a rushed attempt now could cost you the next cycle's start. Check each firm's own rule; most publish none.

screens.prose: Some batteries use negative marking: +1 for right, −1 for wrong, four options. The reported 80 in 8 in l4 works this way (October 2026). Is a blind guess worth taking?
screens.question: What is a blind guess worth on average, in marks?

hints.text: Expected value: chance right times +1, plus chance wrong times −1.
Right with chance 1/4, wrong with chance 3/4.
$\tfrac14 \times 1 + \tfrac34 \times (-1) = -\tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh +1 and −1 by their chances.

byKey.nopen: You counted only the right answers. Each wrong one also costs a mark.
byKey.zero: You assumed a guess is free. With four options you are wrong three times in four.
byKey.onlyneg: You counted only the penalty. A quarter of guesses still score +1.
byKey.sign: A guess is right a quarter of the time and wrong three quarters, so 1/4 − 3/4 is below zero. A positive 0.5 takes 3/4 − 1/4, as if guessing paid.

explain.text: A blind guess is right a quarter of the time: $\tfrac14 - \tfrac34 = -0.5$. As a check, 100 blind guesses give about 25 right and 75 wrong, net −50. Mental Maths Under Pressure trains this later, in "Guessing when wrong answers cost".

screens.prose: The table is now complete. Ruling options out raises the value of a guess. In the reported 80 in 8 you cannot skip, so every item gets an answer.
screens.question: In a test that allows skipping, when does a guess stop costing marks on average?

options.text: Once two options are ruled out, a guess costs nothing on average

options.why: You guessed blind. On average that loses half a mark a time.

options.text: Never; guessing is always a loss
options.why: You never guess. With two ruled out it is even, and with three it gains a mark.

options.text: Once one option is ruled out
options.why: You stopped at one. Three options left still lose a third of a mark.

hints.text: Read the expected marks column.
Where does it reach 0?
With two ruled out it is 0; with three, +1. Before that, a guess loses.

feedback.correct: Two ruled out: an even bet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the expected marks reach zero.

explain.text: A guess breaks even with two options ruled out and gains with three. Where skipping is banned, a forced blind guess still loses 0.5 on average. That is why speed matters: fewer forced guesses.

screens.prose: Timing sets your pace. Two formats reported in l4 (October 2026): 80 arithmetic items in 8 minutes; 17 harder items in 60 minutes.
screens.question: In the 17-item test, how many minutes is that per item? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: Time divided by items.
60 minutes over 17 items.
$60 / 17 \approx 3.53$ minutes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the minutes by the items.

byKey.inv: You divided items by minutes. Divide minutes by items.
byKey.secs: That is in seconds. Give minutes.

explain.text: $60 / 17 \approx 3.53$ minutes, and the reported items get harder, so bank time on the early ones. The arithmetic battery gives $480 / 80 = 6$ seconds an item. Short attention games are also reported (l4); they are proprietary, and the app does not imitate them.

screens.prose: Proctored tests reportedly watch for signs of help. Here is one candidate's room on the day.

rows: Often off screen, reading a sheet

screens.question: Select all that apply: which could a proctored test flag?

options.text: Looking away from the screen often

options.why: You flagged the charger. Staying plugged in is good practice.
You flagged water. It is not a sign of help.

hints.text: What could look like outside help?
Notes, a phone, another person.
The monitor, the phone, the flatmate and the wandering eyes.

feedback.correct: Four things that look like help.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep what could look like outside help.

explain.text: Proctoring looks for a second screen, a phone, another person and eyes that leave the screen. Calculator rules differ by firm (l4, October 2026): one reported test allows one, another is mental. Read the rules for each test.

screens.prose: The morning of the test. Put the steps in the order that leaves you fresh and set up when the clock starts.
screens.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Read the email and the rules again
Set up the room: door shut, phone away
Eat and drink something once the set-up is done
Do a full mock test straight before
lines.why: You did a full mock first. It tires you before the real one; arrive fresh.

hints.text: Rules first, then the room, then the machine.
The system check needs the room set up.
Email, room, system check, eat, start. No mock.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step sets up the next.

byKey.mock: You kept the full mock. It spends your focus before the test that counts.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step that belongs. Only the mock goes.

explain.text: The rules tell you what the room needs. The system check runs in the room you will use. Food comes once the set-up is done, so you start alert with nothing left to fix.

screens.prose: A friend says: "Take the real test once to see the format, then prepare properly." The firm's rule is no retake for 8 months.

rows: See the format on the real link

screens.question: What do you do?

options.text: Practise on mocks and any practice test the firm offers; sit the real link once, prepared
Take it once to see the format
options.why: You chose to take it once to see the format.

options.text: Wait until the last day to sit it, to prepare longest
options.why: You waited. Under rolling review (l3), places fill before the deadline.

options.text: Sit it, then ask for a reset if it goes badly
options.why: You planned on a reset. A reset is for a technical failure, not a bad score.

hints.text: What does "once" mean when there is no retake?
The format-check sitting is the real attempt.
Practise on mocks; sit the real link once, ready.

feedback.correct: The real link is never practice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many attempts you get.

byKey.see: You chose to take it once to see the format. That sitting is your real attempt, and its score stands for 8 months.
byKey.ask: You planned to ask for a reset after a bad score. Firms grant resets for technical faults, not for bad days.

explain.text: The first sitting is the one that counts. With no retake for 8 months, a trial run can cost the cycle. Practise on mocks and the firm's own practice test, if it has one.

screens.prose: An edge case. Twenty minutes in, your connection drops. The test window shows an error when you return.

rows: Back online; the test shows an error

screens.question: What do you do?

options.text: Screenshot the screen and the time, email the recruiter at once, and ask for a reset
Open the link again and start a second copy
options.why: You started again without asking. A second sitting may count as a retake or be flagged.

options.text: Wait a week, then mention it
options.why: You waited. Report a fault at once, while the logs are fresh.

options.text: Say nothing and hope it saved
options.why: You stayed silent. The recruiter cannot fix what they do not know about.

hints.text: What evidence would the recruiter need?
The screen and the time.
Screenshot, email the recruiter now, ask for a reset; never sit a second copy unasked.

feedback.correct: Evidence, then the recruiter, at once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Report it straight away, with evidence.

explain.text: A screenshot with the time shows a technical fault, not a bad attempt. Email the recruiter at once and ask for a reset. Never sit a second copy without asking, because it may count as your retake.

screens.prose: **Follow-up.** Formats change. A new test has five options, +1 for right and −0.25 for wrong. Pace: work it out in your head in under a minute.
screens.question: What is a blind guess worth now, in marks?

hints.text: Same method: weigh each outcome by its chance.
Right with chance 1/5, wrong with chance 4/5.
$\tfrac15 \times 1 + \tfrac45 \times (-0.25) = 0.2 - 0.2 = 0$.

feedback.correct: Zero: the penalty is set so blind guessing breaks even.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the new chances and the new penalty.

byKey.old: You used the old format. Here there are five options and the penalty is a quarter.
byKey.nopen: You counted only the right answers. Wrong ones cost 0.25 each.
byKey.onlyneg: You counted only the penalty. A fifth of guesses score +1.

explain.text: $\tfrac15 - \tfrac45 \times 0.25 = 0.2 - 0.2 = 0$: the penalty is set so blind guessing breaks even. Rule out one option and a guess is worth $\tfrac14 - \tfrac34 \times 0.25 = \tfrac1{16}$. Always read the scoring before the first item.

screens.prose: Nadia, the invented candidate, has three assessment links. The order she sits them in is her choice.
screens.question: Which should she sit first?

options.text: Firm B: the same format, with less at stake
Firm A, to get the most important one done
options.why: You sat the top choice first. Its attempt should come after practice under real conditions.
You picked a different format. Bank C's video does not practise the battery.
You stacked them. A tired third sitting is a wasted attempt.

hints.text: Which sitting is the best practice for the one that matters most?
Same format, less at stake.
Firm B: same style, lower stakes, and it is due first.

feedback.correct: Firm B first. You plan your own test mornings in homework 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Practise under real conditions where less is at stake.

explain.text: Firm B's battery is real practice for Firm A's, with less at stake, and it is due first. Mental Maths Under Pressure and the planned mock assessments train the battery later. You plan your own test mornings in homework 2.

ideas: Check four parts before any test: proctoring, retake rules, timing and the environment.
At +1 and −1 with four options, a guess is worth −1/2, −1/3, 0 or +1. It rises as you rule options out.
The real link is never practice. If it breaks, screenshot, email the recruiter and ask for a reset.
summary.trap: "Take it once to see the format": that sitting is your attempt, and the score stands.

quiz.question: 80 items in 8 minutes. How many seconds is that per item?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn 8 minutes into seconds first.

byKey.min: That is in minutes. Give seconds.
byKey.ten: You divided 80 by 8. Divide the seconds by the items.

explain.text: Eight minutes is 480 seconds, and $480 / 80 = 6$. As a check, 10 items a minute is 6 seconds each.

quiz.question: Four options, +1 right, −1 wrong. You have ruled out two. What is a guess worth on average?

options.why: You counted only the right half. The wrong half costs a mark each time.
That is a blind guess with four options left.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two options left, one right.

explain.text: With two left, $\tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0$. It costs nothing on average, and gains with a third ruled out.

quiz.question: Your connection drops halfway through a proctored test. What comes first?

options.text: A screenshot of the screen with the time
Starting a second copy of the test
options.why: You restarted without asking. It may count as a retake.

options.text: Asking a forum what to do
options.why: You asked strangers. The recruiter is the one who can reset it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What will the recruiter need?

explain.text: A screenshot with the time is the evidence a recruiter needs to grant a reset. Then email them straight away.

quiz.question: A firm allows no retake within 8 months. You sit its test on 1 December 2026. When can you next sit it?

options.why: You counted 6 months.
You counted 12 months.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count 8 months from December.

explain.text: December plus 8 months is August: 1 August 2027. Summer 2028 postings open about a month before that.
